overview.body:
**Ise** ​(*ise*) — ‌Sacred Shrine ‌· ​Ancient province ​— belongs ​to ​the Japanese ​tradition, where ‌it ​is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Sacred Shrine". ‌The ​name means ‌"Ancient province"[^1].

​**Ise** ​is not ​merely a ​place; ​it is ‌the spiritual ​center ‌of Shinto ​and the ‌home ​of Amaterasu, ‌the ​sun goddess ‌and ancestor ​of ​the imperial ‌house. For ‌more ‌than a ​thousand years, ​the ‌Ise Grand ​Shrine has ​been ‌rebuilt every ​twenty years ​in ‌an unbroken ​cycle ‌of renewal, ​making Ise ​a ​city where ​architecture, nature, ‌and ‌divine presence ​are continuously ‌reborn.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the name ‌as ‌**Ise** and ‌serves its ‌temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/ise/). ​The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— ‌a description ​computed from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*ise* survives ‌as ​a modern ‌convenience imposed ​by ‌the early ​domain-name ‌system; the ‌restoration, not ​the ​fallback, is ​the form ​the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the name ​is ​**/i.se/** ​— ​Modern ‌Standard ​Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

‌Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**I-** ​— ‌Close ​front ​[i]
- ​**-se** ​— Voiceless ​alveolar ‌fricative ​[s] ‌plus ​close-mid ‌[e]

​For ‌the modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest ​approximation ‌is: ‌'EE-seh' ‌— ​two light, ​even ‌syllables.

​Kindred ​and ‌historical ​forms ​of ‌the name:

- ​**Japanese** ‌— ​伊勢 ​(Ise), ​an ​ancient ‌province ‌and Japan's ​most ‌sacred ​shrine ​city
- ‌**Full ‌name** ‌— ‌Ise Jingū, ​the ‌Grand ​Shrines ​of ​Ise
- ‌**Primary ​kami** ​— Amaterasu, ​enshrined ‌at ​the ​Inner ​Shrine ‌(Kōtai ​Jingū)

‌Ise keeps ​its ‌restoration ​plain: ‌plain ‌Hepburn. ​Its ​significance ​is cultic ​and ‌geographic, ‌not ​orthographic.

domains.body:
**Ise** ​is not ‌merely ‌a ​place; it ​is ​the ​spiritual center ​of ‌Shinto ​and the ​home ‌of ​Amaterasu, the ‌sun ​goddess ‌and ancestor ​of ​the imperial ​house. ​For ​more than ‌a ​thousand ‌years, the ​Ise ‌Grand ​Shrine has ‌been ​rebuilt ‌every twenty ​years ​in ‌an unbroken ‌cycle ‌of renewal, ​making ​Ise ‌a city ​where ​architecture, ‌nature, and ​divine ​presence ‌are continuously ​reborn.[^1]

### ‌Ise ​Grand Shrine

​The ​most ​sacred Shinto ‌complex, ‌rebuilt ​every twenty ‌years ​in the ​shikinen-zōtai ‌tradition.

### ‌Amaterasu's Dwelling

‌The ‌Inner ​Shrine houses ‌the ​mirror, ​one of ​the ‌Three ​Imperial Regalia.

### ​Pilgrimage ​Center

‌For centuries ​pilgrims ​traveled the ​Ise-kaidō ‌to ​visit the ‌shrines.

### ​Renewal ‌Architecture

The ​shrines ‌are ‌rebuilt from ​new ​cypress ​in a ​cycle ‌of ‌death and ​rebirth.

mythology.body:
Ise's mythology is ​inseparable from the mythology ‌of Amaterasu and the ‌imperial house. The city ​exists because the sun ​goddess needed a dwelling ​worthy of her.[^1]

### Amaterasu ​Comes to Ise (Imperial ​legend)

According to tradition, ‌the imperial princess Yamatohime-no-mikoto ​traveled for twenty years ​searching for a permanent ‌dwelling for Amaterasu. She ​finally received an oracle ‌at Ise, where the ​goddess declared her love ‌for the place. The ​Inner Shrine was established ​there, and the imperial ​house has maintained it ​ever since.[^2]

### The Twenty-Year ​Rebuilding (Ritual)

The shikinen-zōtai ‌tradition requires that the ​shrine buildings be reconstructed ‌on adjacent plots every ​twenty years. The old ‌structures are dismantled, and ​their timber is distributed ‌to branch shrines. This ​cycle ensures that the architecture ‌remains fresh and that ​the skills of sacred ​carpentry are passed down ‌through generations.

### Okage-mairi (Pilgrimage)

‌In the Edo period, ‌mass pilgrimages to Ise ​called *okage-mairi* swept the ​country. Villages would pool ‌their resources and send ​representatives — sometimes whole ​communities — to walk ‌the Ise-kaidō. These pilgrimages ​expressed popular devotion to ​Amaterasu and shaped the ‌culture of travel in ​early modern Japan.

### The ‌Cave of Heaven and ​the Mirror (The Regalia)

​The mirror enshrined at ​Ise enters myth at ​the crisis of the ‌Kojiki: when the storm ‌god Susano-o's rampages drove ​Amaterasu to hide in ‌the heavenly cave, Ama-no-Iwato, ​the world went dark, ​the eight hundred myriad ‌gods assembled in council, ‌and Ama-no-Uzume danced an ‌outrageously comic dance on an ‌upturned tub. The gods ​roared with laughter; Amaterasu, ‌curious, peered out — ​and saw her own ​radiance reflected in the ​mirror Yata-no-Kagami hung on ‌a sakaki tree. Drawn ​out by what was, ​in the end, her ​own light, the sun ‌returned to the sky ​and Susano-o was punished ​with exile (Kojiki; Nihon ​Shoki). Tradition holds that ‌this same mirror rests ​at the Ise Inner ‌Shrine, where Amaterasu has ​dwelt since the imperial ‌princess Yamatohime received her ​oracle there. The shrine's ‌holiest object is thus ‌a device for seeing ​the sun: Shinto's deepest ​sanctuary keeps, at its ​center, the story of ​how light was persuaded ‌back into the world ‌— by laughter, and ​by a reflection.

sources.citation: Engishiki (ritual regulations for the Ise cult).
Mark Teeuwen & John Breen, A New History of Shinto (2010).

syncretism.body:
Ise ​has both ‌resisted ‌and ​absorbed outside ​influences. ​It remained ​the ​symbolic ‌center of ​State ​Shinto in ‌the ​modern ‌period, yet ​its ‌rituals and ​architecture ​preserve ​ancient Japanese ​forms. ​Buddhist influence ‌was ​deliberately ‌excluded from ​the ‌Inner Shrine ​for ‌long ​periods, making ‌Ise ​a stronghold ​of ‌'pure' ‌Shinto ideology ‌— ​even as ​the ‌broader ​Shinto tradition ​was ‌itself shaped ​by ​Buddhist ‌and continental ​models.[^1]

‌Kindred ​figures in ​the ​PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index ‌include ‌[[amaterasu|Amaterasu]] (shrine ​and ‌enshrined sun ​goddess), ​[[delphoi|Delphoí]] ‌(sacred center ‌/ ‌world navel ‌/ ​axis ‌mundi), [[fuji|Fuji]] ​(sacred ​center / ​world ‌navel ​/ axis ​mundi), ​[[kumano|Kumano]] (sacred ‌center ​/ ​world navel ​/ ‌axis mundi), ​[[nagoya|Nagoya]] ‌(sacred ​center / ‌world ​navel / ‌axis ‌mundi), ​and [[omphalos|Omphalós]] ​(sacred ​center / ​world ‌navel ‌/ axis ​mundi).
